implementation_notes: Ruby's constructor is itself a method (Class#new calls allocate and then initialize), so the factory method is simply a class method that picks the class or computes the arguments and calls new - the same shape as Kernel's conversion methods Integer(), Array() and Hash(), which return a converted instance rather than a new object of a named class, and as File.open, which may take a block. What replaces the classic Creator subclass hierarchy is that single class method plus private_class_method :new when callers should not construct directly; the classic structure survives only where a framework already subclasses the creator, and overriding Class#new is a whole-class policy change rather than a per-hierarchy factory.
code_sketch:
class Duration
  def self.from_iso8601(text)      # factory: parses, then constructs
    new(parse_seconds(text))
  end

  def self.seconds(n)              # named constructor
    new(n)
  end

  private_class_method :new        # callers go through the factories
end

Duration.from_iso8601("PT1H30M")
pitfalls: private_class_method :new is a convention with sharp edges: send, allocate plus a manual initialize, subclassing and Marshal.load all bypass it.
A class method that hard-codes the class name instead of using new (or self) breaks subclasses and misleads callers who expect the receiver's type.
Ruby's open classes mean a factory can be redefined at run time by a gem, refinement or monkey patch; keep concrete-class selection in one file and freeze the class where possible.
Kernel-style conversion methods must respect the to_int/to_str protocol (call the conversion method rather than the raw value) or they silently accept/skip values other code expects to be rejected.
